blocks.content: The orange cat in the antique shop window has never acknowledged me. Not once in two years. I pass that window every morning and every morning the cat looks through me like I'm not there, or like I am there and it simply doesn't matter.
I find that easier to be around than most things.

The bookstore two blocks down doesn't open until ten. The window display has a ceramic owl in it that I'm fairly certain has been there since before I moved to this neighborhood. Nobody changes it. I've stopped expecting them to.

Mrs. Okafor was at the corner of Bellamy with her dog, same as every morning. The dog lifted his head when I passed. Mrs. Okafor was looking at her phone. I've never learned the dog's name, which is probably a thing I should fix.

I'm nineteen and freelance, which sounds freer than it is. It means I paint what people ask me to paint and try to make enough from it to keep painting. Last week I finished a commission — a motorcycle floating in outer space, chrome catching light from imaginary stars — and the guy cried when he saw it. I charged him two hundred dollars. Probably should have charged more, but he cried, and I didn't have the heart.

I don't know yet if being a painter means being the person who makes what people need, or if it means something else entirely. I've been thinking about it for three years and I'm not closer to an answer.
The Copper Mug was at the end of the block, its windows lit up against the gray of the morning.
